transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Reyes (Redwood SE), Jen Park (Redwood CSM), Samir Gupta (Avalon - Head of ML), Lina Torres (Avalon - Infra), Ethan Moore (Avalon - PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Avalon is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for predictable latency at peak hours. Their pattern is a daily two-hour peak where latency needs to be sub-200ms for short responses and 1-2s for longer streaming. Interested in reserved GPUs with tenant fencing and a hybrid prewarm/peak-shift burst approach that shifts heavy batch workloads to off-peak windows. Security checks: SOC2, KMS integration, on-prem as a fallback.

Topics:
- Peak-shift bursting and cost smoothing
- Dedicated topology (hot vs warm pools)
- Isolation (tenant fencing, node-level segregation)
- Prewarm, prefix cache, and KV cache behavior
- Fallbacks to hosted models & SLOs

Action items (auto extracted, manual below may differ):
- Redwood to propose benchmark plan
- Avalon to share traces and token distribution

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Olivia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Olivia with Redwood, AE for your account. quick round robin?
[00:10] Samir Gupta: Hi Samir here. head of ML at Avalon. Lina and Ethan from infra and product as well.
[00:16] Lina Torres: Lina, infra.
[00:18] Ethan Moore: Ethan, product.
[00:20] Marco Reyes: Marco, solution engineer, i'll drive the technical parts.
[00:25] Olivia Chen: Great. High level Samir, you shared a one-pager before the call — want to expand on the peak windows and what success looks like?
[00:33] Samir Gupta: Sure. So we have this very sharp daily peak — roughly 11:30 to 13:30 UTC — where traffic spikes 6x, mostly short chat completions for our consumer app. Acceptable p95 latency is under 300ms for short responses (under 120 tokens), and for long-form streaming we can accept up to 1.5s in most cases. Cost is a big factor, we want to avoid paying 24/7 for full hot capacity.
[01:01] Olivia Chen: Understood, so you're leaning to reserved capacity for predictability but want a cost-smoothing approach. Tell us about burst characteristics — is it sustained for the two hours or sudden stomps?
[01:12] Samir Gupta: It's a mix. The first 15 minutes ramp up very quickly, then it plateaus for about 90 minutes with small micro-bursts inside. We also have batch jobs later at night that could run if we shift them.
[01:24] Marco Reyes: ok so this is a classic peak-shift opportunity — move non-urgent batch to off-peak and have a warm prewarm pool to absorb ramp. A few quick questions: what's your model family (GPT-like, open weights) and do you stream tokens or use sync completions?
[01:38] Lina Torres: We're running an in-house finetuned open LLM — roughly 30B parameters, quantized to 4-bit in some paths. Most endpoints use streaming for longer responses but the bulk is short sync calls.
[01:49] Marco Reyes: good — that helps. When we talk about Dedicated, there are a few levers: reserved GPU pool size, hot pool prewarmed instances, and a warm pool that can be prewarmed to a degree or cold started. Also routing rules to fallback to hosted smaller models or lower-precision variants if dedicated capacity hits limits.
[02:05] Ethan Moore: can you explain warm vs hot in practice and the cost delta?
[02:09] Marco Reyes: Sure. hot nodes are fully prewarmed with model weights loaded and KV cache ready — they deliver the lowest latency but cost more because they consume RAM/GPU hours. warm nodes have model artifacts available but may need a small load and weight sync; they can hit warm latency in 10-30s depending on model size and infra. cold nodes are the slowest and require full load ~2-4 minutes. you can also do partial prewarm (shared cold + small KV warm) to trade somewhere in the middle.
[02:36] Samir Gupta: 10-30s is too long for our ramp — we need something faster for the 15-minute ramp. is there a way to pre-emptively prewarm before the window?
[02:45] Marco Reyes: yes — that's the peak-shift idea. schedule prewarm jobs to ramp up hot pool 10 minutes before predicted peaks; we can also use predictive autoscale if you give us historical traces. For burst beyond reserved, Redwood can burst to a reserved overflow, or fall back to hosted models with a different cost profile.
[03:02] Lina Torres: how does isolation work? we can't have other tenants on the same GPU due to compliance.
[03:07] Marco Reyes: We offer node-level fencing on Dedicated — you can reserve whole GPUs for your tenant. For extra assurance we can do dedicated racks in private deployments; that said, node-level fencing is typical and supports KMS integration and audit logs.
[03:22] Samir Gupta: and encryption at rest? we need KMS to manage model keys and patient PII — i mean user PII — nothing PHI but still sensitive.
[03:33] Jen Park: On the Private offering we integrate with customer KMS/HSM, and for Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS via keywrap and audit trails. We'll share the SOC2 artifact as well.
[03:43] Ethan Moore: fallback to hosted — is data sent to hosted endpoints? that's a hard no for us for production PII paths.
[03:49] Marco Reyes: Great question. You can configure routing rules by route or token type: PII routes always stick to Dedicated/Private; non-sensitive routes can fall back to hosted. Redwood's routing policy engine can mark certain models or endpoints as not eligible for fallback.
[04:04] Samir Gupta: our ops team is worried about cold starts during an unexpected surge. Can Redwood do a warm-standby in another region?
[04:12] Marco Reyes: Yes, you can have regional warm pools. We also support KV cache replication strategies to reduce warm-up. There's a tradeoff — multi-region warm pools increase cost but add resilience.
[04:24] Olivia Chen: can you share an example topology for the kind of peak-shift you described? maybe a 2-tier hot/warm + burst to hosted?
[04:31] Marco Reyes: i'll sketch one and put it in the follow-up diagram. quick sketch: reserved hot pool sized for p95 baseline, warm pool sized for +30% capacity that can be prewarmed pre-peak, scheduled batch jobs shifted to off-peak; overflow policy to small hosted model or low-precision variants.
[04:47] Lina Torres: low-precision variants — are you talking quantized variants we can serve on the same GPU?
[04:52] Marco Reyes: yes, if you have a 4-bit quantized variant it's often cheaper and faster; we can host multiple variants and route by request size or latency tolerance.
[05:02] Ethan Moore: what's the SLA on Dedicated? we need an idea for contractual uptime and latency SLOs.
[05:07] Olivia Chen: Our Dedicated plans come with an SLA for uptime and latency targets; we'll share the SLA PDF. for latency SLOs we measure tail latency per model and provide dashboards.
[05:16] Samir Gupta: walk me through a failure case: say our hot pool saturates and hosted fallback is not allowed for certain routes, how do you keep the app functional?
[05:27] Marco Reyes: multiple options: 1) queueing and graceful degradation with a circuit-breaker in the client; 2) automatic model-variant fallback to a smaller local model; 3) surge preemption policies that temporarily reassign warm nodes to hot; 4) reserved overflow purchase as a committed buffer. We'll work with your SREs to define priority and throttles.
[05:45] Lina Torres: re: billing — if we do peak-shift and run batch at night, can we get credits or discounted night usage?
[05:52] Olivia Chen: That can be part of a reserved contract — commit to X monthly GPU-hours and we can shape pricing across day/night usage. We'll outline options in the pricing doc.
[06:03] Ethan Moore: curious about observability — can we get token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency traces?
[06:09] Jen Park: yes, Redwood Console provides per-route cost, token-level breakdown, traces, and can export to your observability stack. we also have tracing hooks for sampling.
[06:18] Samir Gupta: about the benchmark — what's the typical scope?
[06:21] Marco Reyes: We usually run a 72-hour benchmark that includes steady-state load, ramp tests, and synthetic micro-bursts mirroring your traces. We'll simulate your token mix, model variants, and streaming patterns. aim is to validate latency SLO and tail behavior while measuring costs.
[06:36] Ethan Moore: will we need to give you real traffic or can we use synthetic?
[06:39] Marco Reyes: both are fine — synthetic is easier to start. for best results, provide anonymized traces so we can tune prewarm timing and batching profiles.
[06:48] Samir Gupta: any gotchas with KV cache and streaming where cache hits drop latency? we saw something in internal tests where the K-V cache warm-up made the first few requests slow.
[06:58] Marco Reyes: yeah the first prefix misses are common. we recommend prefix warming during prewarm window or sticky sessions routed to hot nodes. also checkpointed KV snapshots can be used to reduce first-request penalty. sometimes transcriptions turn K-V to "K V" or "K-V cash" in notes, so just call it KV cache.
[07:16] Lina Torres: how granular is RBAC and audit logs? we need to show auditors who accessed what model and when.
[07:22] Jen Park: RBAC supports per-team, per-route, and per-model roles; audit logs include API keys, timestamps, and request IDs and are exportable to SIEMs. we'll attach a sample audit output.
[07:35] Ethan Moore: what's the effort to migrate to a Private deployment later if we start with Dedicated?
[07:41] Marco Reyes: migration is straightforward — same API and config, the control plane moves to a VPC/private control plane. stateful artifacts like KV snapshots need migration steps, but we have runbooks. also model artifacts can be pre-staged.
[07:53] Samir Gupta: security question — on Dedicated, do you guys run the control plane in your cloud or can we run the control plane in our VPC?
[07:59] Marco Reyes: Dedicated has a hosted control plane but we offer Private for customer-managed control plane in VPC or on-prem. some customers start on Dedicated and then move to Private for compliance.
[08:10] Olivia Chen: back to cost — would a hybrid approach (small reserved hot pool + larger warm pool + selective hosted fallback) be the sweet spot?
[08:18] Marco Reyes: that's often the most cost-effective if you can tolerate selective fallbacks for non-sensitive paths. given Avalon constraints, we'd probably recommend a larger hot pool for PII endpoints and fallback allowed for anonymized routes.
[08:31] Lina Torres: let's talk numbers — what would a starting hot pool look like for our 30B quantized model with 6x peak?
[08:37] Marco Reyes: rough math: if steady baseline requires 6 GPUs for p95, peak 6x might suggest 36 GPUs peak. But with peak-shift and prewarming plus batching and model variants, you might get away with 20-24 reserved GPUs plus a warm pool that covers additional spikes and scheduled burst windows. we'll run the benchmark to refine.
[08:55] Samir Gupta: 36 to 24 is a big gap — what's the major levers to reduce reserved count?
[08:59] Marco Reyes: batching (teacher), KV cache hit rate, model quantization, and smart routing. For short responses batching isn't as effective, but prefix caching and sticky sessions help. Also shifting batch jobs to night lowers owner's reserved need.
[09:12] Ethan Moore: curious — are there CPU-bound request patterns we need to watch, or is everything GPU-bound?
[09:17] Marco Reyes: mostly GPU-bound for generation, but orchestrator and preprocessing (tokenization) use CPU; we size controllers and tokenizers separately. we'll include those numbers in topology.
[09:28] Samir Gupta: let's cover a scenario: unexpected 20% sustained higher-than-expected load for 3 hours during peak — how does Redwood respond?
[09:36] Marco Reyes: automatic autoscale will attempt to spin additional warm nodes, preemptively convert warm to hot, and apply overflow rules. if fallback disabled for some routes, then you'll see increased queueing; we'll also trigger on-call alerts and can provision burst capacity in short order if contractual buffer exists.
[09:51] Lina Torres: what about preemption of lower-priority tenants — do you do preemption in multi-tenant racks?
[09:57] Marco Reyes: for Dedicated, tenant fencing prevents cross-tenant preemption; in a shared hosted environment lower priority jobs may be preempted, but in Dedicated you control preemption policies inside your own reserved quota.
[10:08] Olivia Chen: any compliance blockers you foresee?
[10:10] Samir Gupta: just the hosted fallback as we said — need to classify which routes are PII and block them from leaving Dedicated. otherwise SOC2 and KMS integration should cover it. We might also need a minimal on-prem path for certain customers next year.
[10:24] Marco Reyes: noted. we'll include a line item in the follow-up doc for on-prem migration path and when it's recommended.
[10:31] Ethan Moore: can we get a mock SLA that includes latency SLOs for p50/p95/p99 per-route?
[10:37] Olivia Chen: yes — we'll include sample SLO tables in the packet.
[10:41] (cross talk)
[10:42] Samir Gupta: quick question — have you integrated with our SSO (Okta)?
[10:45] Jen Park: yes, Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. we'll capture a checklist for Okta integration.
[10:52] Marco Reyes: i wanted to call out one technical note — shipping KV snapshots between regions during prewarm has some consistency cost; we recommend per-region prefills for lowest tail latency.
[11:05] Lina Torres: ok that makes sense.
[11:07] Olivia Chen: time for a quick recap and concrete next steps — Marco, can you summarize the benchmark scope?
[11:12] Marco Reyes: sure: 72-hour run, includes steady baseline at 1x, ramp tests to 6x peak, micro-bursts, streaming flows, and KV cold->warm cycles. We'll run on a mirrored infra and produce metrics for latency p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and prewarm timing. We'll need anonymized traces and model artifacts (or docker image + weights) if you want exact parity.
[11:36] Samir Gupta: we'll provide traces and a model snapshot for testing.
[11:40] Olivia Chen: i'll send pricing options and a topology diagram. Marco will send the benchmark plan. Jen will attach SOC2 and SSO checklist.
[11:48] Ethan Moore: timeline? we want results in about 2 weeks.
[11:52] Marco Reyes: feasible — benchmark kickoff within 5 business days if we get traces; 10 business days to run and analyze.
[11:59] Samir Gupta: that works.
[12:02] Olivia Chen: any final questions?
[12:04] Lina Torres: just one: does Redwood have a recommended throttling strategy at the client level to avoid cascading failures?
[12:09] Marco Reyes: yes, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breaker per-route, and a token bucket limiter tuned to your p95. We can share sample middleware.
[12:20] (silence)
[12:22] Olivia Chen: perfect. Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the benchmark kickoff.
[12:28] Samir Gupta: thanks all.
[12:30] (meeting ends)
